bullets.title: The Ladder of Inference.
bullets.note: This is a framework for finding common ground, or solvable delusions and divergences, rather than simply arguing over conclusions. Paired with [The Work](https://thework.com/2017/10/four-liberating-questions/) by Byron Katie, it’s also a powerful heuristic for stress-testing your own (often limiting) beliefs. Thanks to [Sheila Heen](https://tim.blog/2021/09/09/sheila-heen/?utm_source=convertkit&utm_medium=convertkit&utm_campaign=5bf) of the Harvard Negotiation Project for introducing me to this concept during [our conversation](https://tim.blog/2021/09/09/sheila-heen/?utm_source=convertkit&utm_medium=convertkit&utm_campaign=5bf) on the podcast.

bullets.section: Person I’m studying in time for Halloween
bullets.title: Washington Irving
bullets.note: From Wikipedia: “Washington Irving is an American short-story writer, essayist, biographer, historian, and diplomat of the early nineteenth century. He is best known for his short stories ‘Rip Van Winkle’ (1819) and ‘The Legend of Sleepy Hollow’ (1820), both of which appear in his collection [_The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent_](https://www.amazon.com/Legend-Sleepy-Hollow-Other-Stories/dp/037575721X/). His historical works include biographies of Oliver Goldsmith, the Islamic prophet Muhammad, and George Washington as well as several histories of fifteenth-century Spain that deal with subjects such as Alhambra, Christopher Columbus, and the Moors.” I’m also reading [_The Sketch Book_](https://www.amazon.com/Legend-Sleepy-Hollow-Other-Stories/dp/037575721X/) before bed this week and next.
